phy-renal-337.why: Nephron tubules have a single epithelial layer that reabsorbs most filtered water and solute while secreting selected substances. Hormones regulate tubular transport, and nephron-associated structures participate in endocrine functions such as renin release and calcitriol production.

notes.A: Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin, and proximal tubular cells produce calcitriol. These functions are associated with the nephron and its vasculature.
notes.B: The tubular wall is largely a single epithelial cell layer whose cell type varies according to the function of each segment.
notes.C: Hormones can regulate transport along the nephron. Aldosterone, for example, increases sodium reabsorption in the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron.
notes.D: Most filtered water, sodium and small nutrients are reabsorbed. The tubules also secrete selected substances such as hydrogen ions and organic anions.

phy-renal-338.why: Antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin, directly controls variable water reabsorption in the collecting ducts. It activates V2 receptors on principal cells, increasing apical aquaporin-2 and decreasing the amount of water excreted.

notes.B: Osmotic control of vasopressin is centred in hypothalamic pathways. The medulla oblongata does not directly set collecting-duct water permeability.
notes.C: Plasma osmolality and effective volume influence vasopressin release. The hormone provides the direct signal to the collecting duct.
notes.D: Plasma sodium contributes to tonicity and can influence vasopressin release. It does not directly insert aquaporin-2.
notes.E: Potassium balance affects renal ion handling and can modify concentrating ability in disease. It is not the principal direct control of water excretion.

phy-renal-339.why: The kidneys regulate water and sodium excretion, which affects circulating volume and blood pressure. They also release renin and regulate acid–base balance by reclaiming bicarbonate and excreting net acid.

notes.A: Renal sodium handling and the renin–angiotensin system influence arterial blood pressure.
notes.B: Changes in tubular water reabsorption determine how much filtered water leaves in the urine.
notes.C: Regulation of sodium and water content helps determine extracellular fluid and blood volume.
notes.D: The kidneys contribute to blood pH by reclaiming bicarbonate and excreting acid as ammonium and titratable acid.

phy-renal-345.why: Acute alcohol intake can suppress vasopressin release, and posterior pituitary injury can reduce its delivery to blood. Both can increase water excretion. Hyperglycaemia past the renal reabsorptive capacity causes glucosuria and osmotic diuresis.

notes.A: Acute alcohol intake can decrease vasopressin release and temporarily reduce collecting-duct water reabsorption.
notes.B: When filtered glucose exceeds reabsorptive capacity, glucose remains in the lumen and increases water loss by osmotic diuresis.
notes.C: Aldosterone promotes distal sodium reabsorption. Increased aldosterone is not a general cause of increased urine volume.
notes.D: Posterior pituitary or stalk injury can impair vasopressin release, increasing excretion of dilute urine.

phy-renal-347.why: Vasopressin increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2, allowing more water to be reabsorbed into the hypertonic medulla. It normally decreases urine volume and allows the urine to become more concentrated.

notes.A: Water removal from tubular fluid generally increases urine osmolality when an adequate medullary gradient is present.
notes.C: Proximal water reabsorption largely follows solute and is not the principal adjustable site for vasopressin.
notes.D: Vasopressin is synthesised in hypothalamic neurons. It is transported to the posterior pituitary for storage and release.
notes.E: Vasopressin mainly regulates water balance. Urinary glucose rises when the filtered load exceeds proximal glucose transport or when that transport is impaired.

phy-renal-352.why: Glomerular capillaries form a filtrate when hydrostatic pressure drives water and small solutes across the filtration barrier into Bowman’s space. This primary urine is modified later by tubular reabsorption and secretion.

notes.A: Water and small solutes are filtered from plasma. The glomerular capillary barrier retains blood cells and most large proteins.
notes.B: Hormones such as renin come from specialised renal cells. The chief function of the glomerular capillary tuft is filtration.
notes.C: Water moves across the glomerular barrier by bulk filtration. Tubular secretion refers to a separate transfer into the nephron lumen.
notes.D: Primary urine is the initial glomerular filtrate entering Bowman’s space before tubular processing.

phy-renal-353.why: Obligatory urine volume depends on how much solute must be excreted and how concentrated the kidney can make the urine. A daily load of about 600 milliosmoles divided by a maximal urine osmolality near 1,200 milliosmoles per kilogram gives roughly 0.5 litres.

notes.A: In 100 millilitres, a typical daily solute load would require a concentration far above normal human concentrating capacity.
notes.B: At a maximal osmolality near 1,200 milliosmoles per kilogram, 300 millilitres cannot carry a typical 600-milliosmole load.
notes.C: About 1.5 litres is a common daily output with ordinary fluid intake. The theoretical minimum for a typical load is lower.
notes.D: A person can produce 2.5 litres with higher intake, but this exceeds the minimum volume needed for typical solute excretion.

phy-renal-354.why: The kidneys receive roughly one fifth of resting cardiac output despite accounting for a small fraction of body mass. This high perfusion per gram provides plasma for filtration and exceeds that of the other listed organs under usual resting conditions.

notes.A: The brain has a high total blood flow and sustained oxygen demand, but its blood flow per gram is below the renal value at rest.
notes.B: The liver receives high total flow through the portal vein and hepatic artery. Because of its larger mass, its usual flow per gram is lower.
notes.D: The heart has high oxygen extraction and can increase coronary flow with effort. Resting flow per gram is lower than for the kidneys.
notes.E: Resting skin perfusion varies strongly with temperature and is usually much lower per gram than renal perfusion.

phy-renal-363.why: A representative glomerular filtration rate in a healthy adult is about 125 millilitres per minute. Over 1,440 minutes this is about 180 litres of filtrate per day. Most is reabsorbed, so final urine output is much smaller.

notes.A: One litre per day is closer to final urine output than to the volume of plasma water filtered before reabsorption.
notes.C: Eighteen litres per day corresponds to a filtration rate of about 12.5 millilitres per minute, far below the standard teaching estimate.
notes.D: Fifty litres a day corresponds to roughly 35 millilitres per minute. This is well below the representative healthy adult value.
notes.E: Eight litres per day represents a very low filtration rate rather than the usual healthy adult daily filtrate volume.

phy-renal-364.why: Vasopressin directly adjusts urine water excretion by activating V2 receptors and increasing aquaporin-2 in collecting-duct principal cells. More water is then reabsorbed, provided a medullary osmotic gradient is present.

notes.B: Hypothalamic neurons synthesise vasopressin. The medulla oblongata does not provide the direct collecting-duct signal.
notes.C: Aldosterone increases distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Vasopressin directly controls variable water permeability.
notes.D: A rise in plasma sodium often raises tonicity and promotes vasopressin release. This is an upstream stimulus.
notes.E: The adrenal cortex produces aldosterone and other steroids. The direct adjustable water-permeability signal comes from vasopressin.

phy-renal-385.why: Parasympathetic fibres in the pelvic nerves contract the detrusor chiefly via muscarinic receptors. Cutting those nerves or giving antimuscarinic drugs weakens detrusor activation and can make bladder emptying less effective.

notes.A: Bladder fullness reaches the sacral cord chiefly through afferents in pelvic nerves. The main detrusor motor pathway is pelvic parasympathetic.
notes.C: Muscarinic agonism can promote detrusor contraction. Blocking these receptors is the more direct way to impair contraction.
notes.D: Alpha-adrenergic blockade can decrease bladder outlet resistance and facilitate flow in some forms of obstruction.
notes.E: Beta-3 receptor activation helps relax the detrusor during filling. Beta blockade is not the standard mechanism for loss of the voiding contraction.

phy-renal-388.why: Chronic kidney failure decreases filtration and excretion of nitrogenous waste. Serum urea usually rises, and uric acid often rises because renal urate clearance falls. Diet, medications and other factors can modify the measured values.

notes.B: Reduced renal urate clearance often increases rather than decreases serum uric acid.
notes.C: Creatinine clearance generally falls as renal filtration is lost, even though tubular secretion can affect the estimate.
notes.D: Vomiting removes gastric acid and can cause alkalosis. It does not predictably worsen the underlying acid–base disorder of kidney failure.
notes.E: Lower dietary protein may reduce dietary acid and nitrogen loads. It is not a usual cause of a worsening renal acid–base disturbance.

phy-renal-392.why: Reducing vasopressin decreases aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting-duct principal cells. The ducts then reabsorb less water, increasing the volume of relatively dilute urine. Acute alcohol intake can produce this effect.

notes.A: Afferent arteriolar constriction lowers perfusion of the glomerulus. It is not the direct response of collecting-duct cells to reduced vasopressin.
notes.B: Lower vasopressin typically increases water diuresis by reducing collecting-duct permeability.
notes.C: Vasopressin promotes water conservation when elevated. Suppressing it has the opposite effect.
notes.D: Efferent arteriolar tone affects filtration and is controlled by factors such as angiotensin II. This is not the primary antidiuretic mechanism.

phy-renal-418.why: Urine formation begins with glomerular filtration. Tubular reabsorption returns selected substances to blood, and tubular secretion moves additional substances into tubular fluid. The amount excreted reflects filtration minus reabsorption plus secretion.

notes.A: Diffusion can contribute to tubular transport, but listing it separately omits reabsorption as a major process.
notes.B: Osmosis and diffusion describe transport mechanisms. This list omits glomerular filtration and net tubular secretion.
notes.D: Paracrine signals help regulate renal function. They are not a substitute for tubular reabsorption in the steps of urine formation.
notes.E: Each of the other lists is incomplete. Some include transport mechanisms or regulatory signals in place of a major net process.

phy-renal-419.why: An adult with ordinary intake commonly produces around 1.5 litres of urine in 24 hours, and about 1.5–2 litres is a reasonable teaching estimate. Output varies with intake, solute excretion and water losses outside the kidney.

notes.A: Five hundred millilitres is closer to an obligatory low volume under typical solute loading than to average daily urine output.
notes.C: Five litres a day is substantially above the usual adult range and can occur with polyuria or high fluid intake.
notes.D: A daily volume near 120–180 litres describes glomerular filtrate before most tubular water is reabsorbed.
notes.E: Fifteen litres per day is far above typical urine output and indicates extreme water or solute diuresis.

phy-renal-420.why: Renal clearance is the virtual volume of plasma from which the kidneys remove a substance per unit time. It equals urine concentration multiplied by urine flow, divided by plasma concentration.

notes.A: Diuresis refers to urine production or increased urine flow. It does not specify removal of a particular substance from plasma.
notes.B: Final urine formation describes the combined nephron processes. Clearance quantifies the net removal of a specific solute.
notes.C: Glomerular filtration rate is the volume of filtrate formed per time. It equals clearance only for an appropriate marker handled by filtration alone.
notes.D: Transport maximum is a rate of saturable tubular transport, generally expressed as amount per time rather than plasma volume per time.

phy-renal-434.why: Antidiuretic hormone is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. The kidney responds to it at V2 receptors. The other options describe substances produced or generated within renal tissue.

notes.A: Renal cyclooxygenase pathways generate prostaglandins that help regulate vascular and tubular function.
notes.B: The renal kallikrein–kinin system generates local kinins by cleaving kininogen. This is local production by processing a precursor.
notes.D: Proximal tubular cells use 1-alpha-hydroxylase to form calcitriol from 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
notes.E: Juxtaglomerular granular cells produce renin and release it when renal perfusion or other signals indicate a need to activate the system.

phy-renal-443.why: Oliguria means abnormally low final urine output. A daily volume below roughly 400–500 millilitres is a common adult definition. Clinical criteria also use output relative to body weight and the duration of low flow.

notes.A: Polyuria is an abnormally large urine volume, commonly more than about three litres a day in adults.
notes.B: Polydipsia means excessive thirst or fluid intake and is distinct from measured urine output.
notes.D: Anuria describes almost no urine output. Its threshold is far lower than the range generally termed oliguria.
notes.E: Glucosuria is the presence of glucose in urine. It does not describe a low urine volume.
